explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The text says this land "…sends couriers by sea, in papyrus vessels on the waters." (Isaiah 18:2) Papyrus boats on the waters means the mail goes out by boat. My cookie boxes only have to cross the counter, so I'm humbled.

Nice try, friend, but there's no camel anywhere in this verse. The text says the couriers go "…by sea, in papyrus vessels on the waters." (Isaiah 18:2) So picture boats and water, not a long dusty trip.

Horses make for a great picture, friend. But the verse never mentions horses or mountain trails. It says the couriers go "…by sea, in papyrus vessels on the waters." (Isaiah 18:2) These messengers are traveling by boat.
Yes, baker! The messengers go to "…a people widely feared…" (Isaiah 18:2) The verse also calls them tall, smooth-skinned and a powerful nation. That's a résumé you'd read twice.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says the messengers go "…to a people widely feared…" (Isaiah 18:2) It sits right next to tall, smooth-skinned and powerful. A fearsome crowd, according to the verse.

Right on the money, baker. The verse says this nation's land is "…divided by rivers." (Isaiah 18:2) It's the same detail the passage repeats in verse 7, so it must matter. Rivers running through the land, like lines of icing on a cookie.
Sand is a fair guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say a word about dunes. It says their land is "…divided by rivers." (Isaiah 18:2) So think water running through the land, not sand piling up.
Snowy peaks sound pretty, but this verse has no snow in it. It says the nation's land is "…divided by rivers." (Isaiah 18:2) Rivers are the whole picture here.

Yes, that's the first blank. "…when a banner is raised on the mountains, you will see it…" (Isaiah 18:3) A banner is something you look at, and a raised one on a mountain is hard to miss. I once lost a whole tray of cookies in plain sight, so I'm no expert.
That's the second blank, baker. "when a ram’s horn sounds, you will hear it." (Isaiah 18:3) A horn is made to be heard. The verse pairs one thing to look at with one thing to listen to.

Touch is a real sense, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The verse says you will "see" the banner and "hear" the horn. (Isaiah 18:3) A banner raised on the mountains is something you look at, not something the verse says you touch.
Tasting a banner is a bold plan, friend. I like the confidence. But the verse says you will "see" the banner and "hear" the horn. (Isaiah 18:3) Neither one goes in the mouth.
Smell is a good sense, and I use it on my cookies every day. It just isn't in this verse. The text says you will "see" the banner and "hear" the horn. (Isaiah 18:3)
That's it, baker. The LORD says, "I will quietly look on from My dwelling place…" (Isaiah 18:4) Notice the word quietly. He looks on from where He dwells, and the verse says it will be quiet.

Battle is a fair guess, friend, but that's not what the verse says. In this message the LORD says, "I will quietly look on from My dwelling place…" (Isaiah 18:4) He looks on quietly from where He dwells. Rushing out to battle isn't mentioned.
That's a dramatic guess, friend. But in this message the LORD says, "I will quietly look on from My dwelling place…" (Isaiah 18:4) No fire is mentioned in this verse. It's a quiet look.

True, baker. The LORD says it is "…like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest." (Isaiah 18:4) Both comparisons are right there in the verse. He gives two pictures for His quiet looking on.

This one is actually true, friend. The LORD says He will quietly look on "…like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest." (Isaiah 18:4) Both comparisons are right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: Cut them off with a pruning knife
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says, "…He will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife…" (Isaiah 18:5) The timing is before the harvest, once the flower has become a ripening grape. It's a picture of a vine being cut back.

explanations.answer: Water them with the morning dew
explanations.explanation: Dew does show up in this passage, friend, but in verse 4, as a comparison for the LORD's quiet looking. In verse 5 the text says, "…He will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife…" So the shoots get cut, not watered.

explanations.answer: Tie them up to a wooden stake
explanations.explanation: Staking a vine is a real thing gardeners do, friend, but it's not in this verse. The text says, "…He will cut off the shoots with a pruning knife…" (Isaiah 18:5) The knife is the whole story here.

I see why you'd hope so, friend, but the text says otherwise. The LORD will "…remove and discard the branches." (Isaiah 18:5) Discard means they're thrown out, not kept safe for later. Not a happy detail.
That's right, baker. The text says He will "…remove and discard the branches." (Isaiah 18:5) Nothing is saved for later. It's a tough picture, and I won't pretend it isn't.

Yes, baker, that's true. The text says, "They will all be left to the mountain birds of prey, and to the beasts of the land." (Isaiah 18:6) It goes on to say the birds will feed on them in summer, and all the wild animals in winter. I think this part is heavy. So take a breath with me.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says, "They will all be left to the mountain birds of prey, and to the beasts of the land." (Isaiah 18:6) It goes on to say the birds feed on them in summer and the wild animals in winter. It's a hard picture, so take a breath.

That's it, baker! "At that time gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts…" (Isaiah 18:7) These gifts come from the same widely feared nation named earlier in the passage. I did NOT see that one coming, and I'm still smiling about it.
Spears are a natural thing to pick, but the verse doesn't mention them. It says, "…gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts…" (Isaiah 18:7) No spears anywhere. Just gifts.

Chariots fit the fearsome picture, friend, but they aren't in this verse. The text says, "…gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts…" (Isaiah 18:7) The surprise is the gifts, brought by the nation people feared.

You got it, baker. The gifts go "…to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts." (Isaiah 18:7) The passage ends there, with a destination. A good place to land after all that talk of knives and branches.

Sinai is a real mountain, friend, but it isn't the one named here. The verse says the gifts are brought "…to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts." (Isaiah 18:7) Same kind of ending, different mountain.

Carmel is a real mountain too, friend, but this verse picks a different one. It says the gifts are brought "…to Mount Zion, the place of the Name of the LORD of Hosts." (Isaiah 18:7) Zion is the name to remember from this passage.
